newsitem.title: USA: Congress sends Clinton budget before deadline.
newsitem.headline: Congress sends Clinton budget before deadline.

text.p: The U.S. Congress handed President Bill Clinton a major victory on Monday by sending him a final budget accord with his top spending priorities intact, just in time to avert a government shutdown.
Clinton successfully demanded an extra $6.5 billion of spending with the lion's share going to his top priority of education.
On an 84-15 vote, the Senate passed the measure only hours before a midnight deadline marking the start of fiscal 1997. The House passed the bill on Saturday, 370-37.
House Republicans, anxious to return home and campaign in the weeks before the November 5 election, abandoned earlier demands to slash spending.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle called the shift a "remarkable retreat from the Republican positions of two years ago, when the majority party in Congress demanded deep cuts in education and the environment and a slowing of Medicare growth that Clinton said would ultimately require cuts in benefits.
Analysts at conservative think tanks agreed.

"Essentiallly the Republicans took this big boulder (of budget cuts) and rolled it 90 percent of the way up hill and then let it fall right back on them," said Steven Moore of the Cato Institute, calling the budget a "big win" for Clinton.

But Republicans calculated that compromise was necessary. They had been blamed for two partial government shutdowns resulting from disagreement over the budget, and saw their popularity evaporate in public opinion polls.

"It's more than we would like to have done but the White House insisted on adding more money for a number of programmes," said Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott. The Mississippi Republican added that the bottom line was that Congress was sending the bill "to the president and he can sign it and the government will be operating tomorrow morning and for the balance of the fiscal year."
Clinton praised the deal as "good for America because it continues to move us toward a balanced budget while protecting, not violating, our values."

The bill funded the military, national parks, education, jobs programmes, environmental protection and law enforcement, the White House, foreign aid, health research, and many other activities, rolling together six spending bills that would be considered separately in an ordinary year.
It also incorporated a once-contentious immigration bill and a badly needed measure to strengthen the thrift insurance fund.
The spending bill provided $244 billion for the military and about $356 billion for other domestic programmes.
